conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your doctor during this stay. You were brought in from rehab because you've been losing weight and not eating well. Can you tell me how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been really weak lately. I can’t even walk without a wheelchair. I eat when I can, but I don’t know why I keep losing weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned chronic diarrhea—how often are you having loose stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three to four times a day, loose and watery. No blood, they checked at rehab. I get bloated if I eat too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll look into that. Your vitals show low blood pressure and you’re very thin, so we’re concerned about malnutrition. We’d like to place a feeding tube to help you gain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A feeding tube? I don’t want another NG tube. They tried that at rehab and I pulled it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This would be a Dobhoff tube—thinner and more comfortable. It goes down to your stomach and we can start tube feeds slowly. It’s temporary while we figure out the best long-term option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, if it helps. But I really don’t feel sick, just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidneys aren’t working as well as they should. Your creatinine is elevated. We’re checking for infection and blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Kidneys again? After my last hospital stay, I thought that was better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re monitoring closely. We’ve sent a urine culture. In the meantime, we’re starting IV fluids and will check with a CT scan to see if there’s a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT results. There’s a new finding—right-sided hydronephrosis, which means your right kidney is swollen due to a backup of urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Swollen kidney? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we think it’s due to a blockage or retention. Your bladder isn’t emptying properly. We’re going to place a Foley catheter to drain it and relieve the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another catheter? I had one before. Is this going to be long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not long-term. Just until we treat the infection and figure out the cause. The CT also showed a bladder diverticulum—like a pouch—which might be trapping urine and causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I keep getting UTIs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll treat the infection now and refer you to urology for a cystoscopy later to look inside your bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your urine culture came back. It’s Klebsiella, but it’s sensitive to many antibiotics. We’re starting IV ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m allergic to penicillin and ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ceftriaxone is a different class. It’s safe for you. We checked your allergies. This should clear the infection and help your kidneys recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Dobhoff tube was placed last night. It’s coiled in your stomach and positioned well. We’re starting slow tube feeds this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel it. That’s better than the last one. Will I still be able to eat by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try small amounts, but the feeds will provide most of your nutrition for now. We want to make sure you gain weight and get stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started mirtazapine yesterday for appetite and mood. How’s your sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still not sleeping well. I take trazodone but it doesn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mirtazapine can help with both. We’ll give it a few days. Psychiatry thinks your lack of motivation might be partly due to mood, even if it’s not classic depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is coming down—from 2.1 to 1.5. That’s a good sign. The Foley is draining well, and your kidney swelling is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the catheter helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it relieved the obstruction. Your kidney function is recovering. We’ll keep the Foley in until your urology visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea is still ongoing. We tested for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter—everything came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’re using a standard formula. We’re sending a fecal fat test to check for malabsorption. That result will come later, and your hepatologist will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin has been slowly dropping. The stool test was positive for blood, but you’re stable and not needing transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t noticed any blood in my stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be microscopic. Given your history and low white count, we’re checking a CMV viral load to rule out infection, especially since you’re on immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like from my liver transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your sirolimus level is therapeutic and liver tests are normal, so no sign of rejection. But CMV can reactivate in transplant patients.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your renal ultrasound today shows the hydronephrosis is gone. Great improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can I get the catheter out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need urology to evaluate why it happened. You still have the diverticulum, which could cause retention again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your TSH came back elevated—15. We’re starting thyroid replacement. That might also help with fatigue and weight gain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I had thyroid issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in liver disease. We’ll monitor it. Also, your electrolytes have been low—magnesium, phosphate. We’re replacing them slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. Creatinine is down to 1.1, you’re tolerating feeds, and your strength is improving. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To extended care. You’ll continue tube feeds and the Foley catheter until your urology visit. You’ll finish two more days of IV antibiotics at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the feeding tube? Will I need it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not forever. Once your nutrition improves, they’ll consider a PEG tube—a permanent one placed in a procedure. But for now, this is helping you heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re stable, standing with help, and doing well on feeds. We’ll go over your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep taking the loperamide for diarrhea, mirtazapine at night, and the heparin shots to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—no QT-prolonging meds like ciprofloxacin. Your heart rhythm is stable, but we’re still cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll tell my doctors. And I’ll follow up with urology and hepatology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They’ll handle the cystoscopy, fecal fat results, and CMV test. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
